summary: Introduces a well-known localEngineID and a discovery mechanism that lets an SNMPv3 application learn the snmpEngineID of a remote SNMP engine. SNMPv3 needs that identifier before it can retrieve or manage objects on a remote entity. It updates RFC 3411 and has Internet Standard status.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMPv3 agents each carry a long identifier, and a manager cannot read anything from an agent until it knows that identifier. This RFC gives the manager a way of asking for it: a special fixed identifier that every agent understands, used once to fetch the real one.

questions: how to find remote snmp engine id
how to discover snmpv3 engine id
what is a snmp context engine id
subtitle: A way for a network manager to learn the identifier of a remote agent before it can query it.

tldr.problem: To read or change anything on a remote SNMPv3 agent, the manager has to know that agent's snmpEngineID, and configuring that identifier on every management application by hand is impractical.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a well-known localEngineID value that always refers to the local default context, and a procedure in which the manager reads the snmpEngineID.0 scalar of the framework MIB using that value, then uses the answer as the contextEngineID for its real requests.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism works with security models that have no discovery of their own, and the format registry that IANA keeps for engine identifiers was given explicit allocation rules.

today: RFC 5343 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted, so the localEngineID value and the discovery procedure it defines remain the way an SNMPv3 application finds the identifier of a remote agent. It updated RFC 3411, which remains the architecture document for the SNMP management framework, and the format registry it clarified is the one IANA still maintains.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
To retrieve or manipulate management information using the third version of the Simple Network Management Protocol, it is necessary to know the identifier of the remote SNMP protocol engine, the so-called snmpEngineID. While an appropriate snmpEngineID can in principle be configured on each management application for each SNMP agent, it is often desirable to discover the snmpEngineID automatically.

This document introduces a discovery mechanism that can be used to learn the snmpEngineID of a remote SNMP protocol engine. The proposed mechanism is independent of the features provided by SNMP security models, and it has been designed to coexist with discovery mechanisms that may exist in SNMP security models, such as the authoritative engine identifier discovery of the User-based Security Model.

The document also updates RFC 3411 by clarifying the IANA rules for the maintenance of the SnmpEngineID format registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Every SNMP agent has its own identifier. The manager needs it before it can ask the agent anything, and nobody wants to write it into the configuration by hand for every device in the network.

sections.title: Engines, Contexts and the Four-Part Name
sections.content:
Within an administrative domain, an SNMP engine is uniquely identified by an snmpEngineID value. An SNMP entity, which consists of an SNMP engine and several SNMP applications, may provide access to multiple contexts. An SNMP context is a collection of management information accessible by an SNMP entity. An item of management information may exist in more than one context and an SNMP entity potentially has access to many contexts.

A context is identified by the snmpEngineID value of the entity hosting the management information, also called a contextEngineID, and a context name that identifies the specific context, also called a contextName. To identify an individual item of management information within an administrative domain, a four tuple is used: a contextEngineID, a contextName, an object type, and its instance identification. The last two elements are encoded in an object identifier value. The contextName is a character string while the contextEngineID is an octet string constructed according to the rules of the SnmpEngineID textual convention.

The SNMP architecture introduces the concept of a scopedPDU as a data structure containing a contextEngineID, a contextName and a protocol data unit, and the SNMPv3 message format uses scopedPDUs to exchange management information.

Within the SNMP framework, contextEngineIDs serve as end-to-end identifiers. This becomes important where SNMP proxies are deployed to translate between protocol versions or to cross middleboxes such as network address translators. In addition, snmpEngineIDs separate the identification of an SNMP engine from the transport addresses used to communicate with it, so management information can be correlated easily even where multiple different transports were used or where transport addresses change dynamically.

The User-based Security Model provides a mechanism to discover the snmpEngineID of the remote engine, since that is needed for security processing reasons, and the discovered value can then be used as a contextEngineID in a scopedPDU. Other security models, such as the Transport Security Model, lack such a procedure and may use the discovery mechanism defined in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Naming one managed item takes four things: which agent hosts it, which group of items inside that agent, what kind of item it is, and which instance. The first two travel in the message header, the last two in the object identifier.

sections.title: The Two Parts of the Mechanism
sections.content:
The discovery mechanism consists of two parts. The first is the definition of a special well-known snmpEngineID value, called the localEngineID, which always refers to a local default context. The second is the definition of a procedure to acquire the snmpEngineID scalar of the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB using that special well-known localEngineID value.

The split matters because the two halves can be used independently. The localEngineID is useful on its own, since it lets a manager address an agent's default context without knowing the agent's real identifier. The discovery procedure uses it as a bootstrap value, so that a manager can find out the real identifier before it needs to use it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two pieces. A fixed identifier that every agent recognises and that means the default collection of information, and a procedure that uses that fixed identifier once to fetch the agent's real identifier.

sections.title: The Local EngineID
sections.content:
An SNMP command responder implementing this specification must register its pduTypes using the localEngineID snmpEngineID value by invoking the registerContextEngineID() abstract service interface defined in RFC 3412. This registration is done in addition to the normal registration under the SNMP engine's own snmpEngineID, which is consistent with the SNMPv3 specifications since they explicitly allow registration of multiple engineIDs and multiple pduTypes.

The SnmpEngineID textual convention defines that an snmpEngineID value must be between 5 and 32 octets long. This specification proposes to use the variable length format 3 of that convention and to allocate the reserved, unused format value 6, using the enterprise ID 0 for the localEngineID. The ASN.1 definition for localEngineID would look like this: localEngineID OCTET STRING ::= '8000000006'H.

The localEngineID value always provides access to the default context of an SNMP engine. It is intended to be used as a special value for the contextEngineID field in the scopedPDU, and it must not be used as a value to identify an SNMP engine. That is, it must not be used in the snmpEngineID.0 scalar or in the msgAuthoritativeEngineID field in the securityParameters of the User-based Security Model.
sections.plainLanguage: The fixed value is five bytes long and is built like any other engine identifier, so no new syntax is needed. It means one thing only: the default collection of information at the receiving agent.

sections.title: The Discovery Procedure
sections.content:
Discovery of the snmpEngineID is done by sending a Read Class protocol operation to retrieve the snmpEngineID scalar using the localEngineID defined above as a contextEngineID value. Implementations should only perform this discovery step when it is needed. In particular, if security models are used that already discover the remote snmpEngineID, such as the User-based Security Model, then no further discovery is necessary. The same is true in situations where the application already knows a suitable snmpEngineID value.

The procedure to discover the snmpEngineID of a remote SNMP engine is described in four steps. First, check whether a suitable contextEngineID value is already known; if so, use the provided value and stop. Second, check whether the selected security model supports discovery of the remote snmpEngineID; if so, let the security model perform the discovery, and if the remote value has been successfully determined, assign it to the contextEngineID and stop. Third, send a Read Class operation to the remote SNMP engine using the localEngineID value as the contextEngineID in order to retrieve the scalar snmpEngineID.0 of the SNMP-FRAMEWORK-MIB; if successful, set the contextEngineID to the retrieved value and stop. Fourth, return an error indication that a suitable contextEngineID could not be discovered.

The procedure outlined above is an example and can be modified to retrieve more variables in the third step, such as the sysObjectID.0 scalar or the snmpSetSerialNo.0 scalar of the SNMPv2-MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: Start with what is already known, then ask the security model, then ask the agent directly. If none of that works, report that the identifier could not be found.

sections.title: The SnmpEngineID Format Registry
sections.content:
RFC 3411 asked IANA to create a registry for SnmpEngineID formats, but did not ask IANA to record the initial assignments made by RFC 3411, nor did it spell out the precise allocation rules. This document establishes those rules.

IANA maintains a registry for SnmpEngineID formats. The first four octets of an SnmpEngineID carry an enterprise number, while the fifth octet in a variable length SnmpEngineID value, called the format octet, indicates how the following octets are formed. The format values allocated in RFC 3411 are 0 for reserved and unused, 1 for an IPv4 address, 2 for an IPv6 address, 3 for a MAC address, 4 for administratively assigned text and 5 for administratively assigned octets, with 6 to 127 reserved and unused and 128 to 255 enterprise specific.

IANA can assign new format values out of the originally assigned and reserved number space 1 to 127, and for new assignments in that number space a specification is required. The number space 128 to 255 is enterprise specific and is not controlled by IANA. Per this document, IANA has made the assignment of format value 6 for the local engine.
sections.plainLanguage: The fifth byte of an engine identifier says what the rest of the identifier is: an address, a hardware address, text chosen by an administrator, and so on. IANA now keeps a list of those meanings, and this document takes one of the reserved values for the local engine.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SNMPv3 provides cryptographic security to protect devices from unauthorized access, and this specification recommends the use of the security services provided by SNMPv3. In particular, it is recommended to protect the discovery exchange.

An snmpEngineID can contain information such as a device's MAC address, IPv4 address, IPv6 address, or administratively assigned text. An attacker located behind a router, firewall or network address translator may not be able to obtain this information directly, and might therefore discover snmpEngineID values in order to obtain this kind of device information.

In many environments, making snmpEngineID values accessible at a security level of noAuthNoPriv will benefit legitimate tools that try to determine basic information about a device. For this reason, the default View-based Access Control Model configuration in RFC 3415 gives noAuthNoPriv read access to the snmpEngineID, and the User-based Security Model discovery mechanism uses unprotected messages and reveals snmpEngineID values. In highly secure environments, snmpEngineID values can be protected by using the discovery mechanism described in this document together with a security model that does not exchange cleartext SNMP messages, such as the Transport Security Model.

The isAccessAllowed() abstract service primitive of the SNMP access control subsystem does not take the contextEngineID into account when checking access rights, so it is not possible to define a special view for context engineID discovery. A request with a localEngineID is thus treated like a request with the correct snmpEngineID by the access control subsystem. This is in line with the SNMPv3 design where the authenticated identity is the securityName, together with the security model and security level information, and transport addresses or knowledge of contextEngineID values do not affect the access control decision.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier can leak a hardware or network address, so the RFC recommends protecting the exchange that fetches it. Note that the access rules cannot tell a discovery request from any other request, because they do not look at the context identifier at all.
